title: DfE Decoded #155 The EYFS Profile Is Changing — But Not in the Way You Might Think
author: A Headteacher's Perspective
summary: The author reads the updated Early Years Foundation Stage Profile handbook and finds its central message is a permission slip rather than a new requirement: written and photographic evidence are not needed, and Reception teachers should be teaching and knowing children rather than documenting proof that learning occurred. Two leadership arguments follow. First, the seventeen Early Learning Goals are a narrow measure and must not be allowed to colonise the Reception curriculum, because nationally assessed statements invite schools to work backwards from the assessment into trackers and highlighted checklists. Second, workload of this kind never arrives as one large demand but accumulates photograph by photograph and upload by upload, which makes it a leadership problem rather than a teacher problem. The piece applies a single test to every recording practice: does this help us teach this child, or does it exist in case someone asks to see it. It also flags that an emerging judgement carries almost no information for a Year 1 teacher, so the handbook's emphasis on passing on identified barriers and the strategies that worked matters more than the label. The author notes that Ofsted gains IDSR access to school-level EYFS data from autumn 2026 and warns that the wrong response would be more tracking, since inspectors will not ask for physical evidence behind individual judgements.
points: The handbook's SEND guidance is read as a corrective to assessors who strip away support to see what a child can do unaided, when those adjustments are part of the child's normal provision.
Best-fit professional judgement against a whole ELG description is contrasted with ticking off individual bullet points, and the author argues school systems must visibly trust teachers to make it.
Transition is recast as the Profile's actual purpose, with professional dialogue between Reception and Year 1 teachers scheduled before the end-of-year rush rather than extra written reports.
The author proposes an audit in reverse: sit with the Early Years team and ask of every tracker, observation and upload why it exists, keeping only what informs teaching.
New Ofsted visibility of three years of GLD outcomes is identified as the moment schools are most likely to add evidence burden for exactly the wrong reason.
quotes: Reception teachers should spend their time teaching, interacting with children, and understanding their learning — not collecting evidence to prove that learning has happened.
Instead, the EYFS Profile should be based primarily on something much more valuable: a teacher knowing their children well.
The DfE describes the ELGs as a narrow measure of children’s development and makes clear that they should not restrict the breadth of the curriculum.
Once something becomes nationally assessed, there is always a danger that we begin working backwards from it.
Are we recording something because it helps us teach the child, or because we feel we need evidence that the child has done it?
Children with SEND should be assessed using the adaptations and adjustments they normally have.
But if those adjustments are part of the child’s normal provision, they remain part of the context in which the child demonstrates what they know and can do.
Every minute a Reception teacher spends proving that learning happened is a minute they can’t spend helping the next bit of learning happen.
